data.content_ref: inline:The claim's central defense against the charge of smuggling in induction is a distinction without a difference. It asserts that 'preference as a rational guess toward truth' is non-inductive while 'expectation of future success' would be inductive. But the mechanism reveals that both are derived from exactly the same evidence — corroboration (past test-survival) — and both rank an unobservable property. The mechanism states: 'A theory with higher empirical content has survived more severe tests, making it a better candidate for being close to the truth (verisimilitude).' This is structurally inductive: it infers from an observed historical fact (survived tests) to an unobserved theoretical property (truth-likeness). Relabeling the target of the inference from 'probability of future success' to 'truth-likeness' does not alter the inferential structure. The claim provides no principled criterion for why one is non-inductive and the other is — it merely stipulates the difference. In any decision-theoretic context, preferring a theory because it is a 'better candidate for being close to the truth' and preferring it because you expect it to perform better lead to identical actions (acting on the preferred theory). The claim's own countercondition 2 ('If acting on a theory inherently requires assigning it a higher subjective probability of success...') identifies this risk but the claim does not resolve it — it only renames the inference's target property.
